why: Most B2B deals are won or lost in discovery, long before the price is discussed. Sales development reps, account executives and key account managers are hired to find a real problem, measure what it costs, qualify honestly and build the demo and the business case on what the client said, not on the product brochure.
outcome: run a discovery call with an upfront contract and a clear next step, ask open, SPIN-style questions that uncover pain and impact, qualify a deal with BANT and MEDDIC / MEDDPICC, map the buying committee, turn the pain into a business case (cost of the problem, ROI, payback), run a tell-show-tell demo and agree a mutual action plan.

lessons.title: Why discovery decides the deal
text: Discovery is the stage where you learn how the client works today, what is not working, what it costs them and how they decide. Product pitching does the opposite: the rep opens with a tour of features and hopes one of them lands. In B2B, where several people sign off on a purchase and a wrong choice is expensive, buyers rarely move because a feature looks nice; they move because a problem they care about has a cost, an owner and a date.

Consultative selling (also called solution selling) puts the client’s problem first. The rep acts like a doctor: diagnose before you prescribe. Questions come before answers, the rep talks less than the client, and the proposal only covers what was found in discovery. Several known methods build on this idea: SPIN Selling (Neil Rackham) for the questions, Sandler for the upfront contract and honest qualification, and The Challenger Sale (Dixon and Adamson) for teaching the client something new about their own business. They differ in style, not in the principle that the client’s situation drives the conversation.

Good discovery protects your time as much as the client’s. It tells you early when there is no real problem, no budget, no one who can decide or no reason to act this year. Disqualifying a deal in week two is a good result: an account executive who carries twenty deals that will never close forecasts badly and has no time left for the five that could.

Discovery is not a single call. The first meeting opens it, but you keep discovering through the cycle: new people join, priorities shift, a competitor appears. Every later stage (the demo, the business case, the proposal, the negotiation) is only as strong as the facts gathered here. When a deal stalls late, the cause is very often a gap that discovery left open: no economic buyer met, no measured impact, no agreed decision process.
points: Diagnose before you prescribe: questions first, product later.
Buyers act on a problem with a cost, an owner and a date, not on a feature.
Disqualifying early is a win: it frees time for deals that can close.
Discovery continues through the whole cycle, not only in the first call.
SPIN, Sandler and Challenger differ in style; all start from the client’s situation.

example.code:
PRODUCT PITCH (weak)
"Thanks for your time. Let me show you our platform: OCR capture,
3-way matching, approval workflows, 40 ERP connectors..."
-> the client nods, says "send me a deck", and the deal goes quiet.

CONSULTATIVE OPENING (strong)
"Thanks for your time. Before I show anything, I'd like to understand
how invoices are processed today and where it hurts. If it looks like
we can help, we agree on a next step; if not, I'll tell you. Fair?"
-> the client talks about 1,200 invoices a month, late payment
   penalties and a team of three working overtime at month-end.
example.note: The second opening earns the facts that the demo and the business case will use.

lessons.title: Running a discovery call
text: Prepare before you dial. Read the company’s website, recent news, job offers (a company hiring three accounts payable clerks has a volume problem) and the contact’s LinkedIn profile. Write three or four hypotheses about what could hurt in their world and the questions that would confirm or kill each one. Preparation lets you skip generic questions the website already answers and shows the client you did your homework.

Open with an upfront contract, a Sandler idea: agree at the start on the time available, the purpose of the call, what each side wants to learn and the possible outcomes, including “this is not a fit”. It takes thirty seconds, removes the pressure of a hidden sales pitch and makes it normal to end the call with a clear yes, no or next step instead of a vague “let’s keep in touch”.

During the call, the client should talk most of the time. Watch your talk ratio: if you speak more than the client in a discovery call, you are pitching. Ask one question at a time, let silences last, and follow up on what you hear (“You said month-end is painful: what happens exactly?”). Take notes in the client’s own words; you will reuse them in the summary, the demo and the proposal.

Close the call with a summary and a next step. Repeat back what you understood (situation, problems, impact, who decides, timing) and ask the client to correct it. Then agree a concrete next step with a date and the people who should attend, and send it in a short follow-up e-mail the same day. A call that ends without a dated next step is the first sign of a stalled deal.

Log everything in the CRM right after the call: contacts and roles, pains in the client’s words, numbers heard, qualification gaps and the next step. The account executive, your manager and later customer success will read it; a discovery that lives only in your head is lost when the deal changes hands.
points: Prepare hypotheses and questions from the website, news, job offers and LinkedIn.
Upfront contract: time, purpose, both agendas and possible outcomes, including “no”.
Keep a low talk ratio: the client talks most of the time.
End with a summary in the client’s words and a next step with a date.
Log the call in the CRM the same day.

example.code:
UPFRONT CONTRACT (first minute)
"We have 30 minutes, is that still OK? My goal is to understand how
your team handles supplier invoices today and what you'd like to
change. You probably want to know whether we've solved this for
companies like yours. At the end, we decide together: a demo with
your finance director, or we agree it's not a fit. Sound good?"

CALL NOTES (client's words)
Situation: 1,200 invoices/month, 3 AP clerks, ERP = SAP Business One
Problem:   "we key everything by hand", "month-end is chaos"
Impact:    ~9 min per invoice, late penalties last quarter
Decision:  CFO signs above 20k EUR, IT must validate the connector
Timing:    new ERP module live in March, wants a fix before
Next step: demo Tue 14 Oct 10:00 with CFO + AP lead (invite sent)
example.note: The notes separate situation, problem, impact, decision and timing, and end with a dated next step.

lessons.title: Questions that uncover pain and impact
text: Open questions (what, how, why, tell me about) make the client explain and reveal things you did not know. Closed questions (yes / no, a number, a choice) confirm facts and close a topic. Discovery uses mostly open questions, with closed ones to check details: “How do invoices reach your team today?” then “So all of them arrive by e-mail as PDFs?”. Avoid leading questions such as “Wouldn’t it be great to save time?”: everyone says yes, you learn nothing and the client feels handled.

SPIN, from Neil Rackham’s research on large sales, sorts questions into four kinds. Situation questions collect facts (volumes, tools, team); ask few of them, because the client gets nothing from answering. Problem questions look for difficulties and dissatisfaction. Implication questions explore the consequences of a problem: what it causes, who else it affects, what it costs. Need-payoff questions let the client say the value of a solution in their own words (“If approvals took one day instead of eight, what would that change for you?”).

Implication questions turn a small annoyance into a business problem. “Invoices are keyed by hand” is a problem; “because of the backlog we missed early-payment discounts and paid late penalties, and the CFO cannot close the month before day 8” is a business problem with a cost and an executive who cares. Ask who is affected beyond the person you are talking to: a problem that touches finance, purchasing and suppliers has more owners and more urgency.

Quantify the impact with the client, not for them. Ask for the volume, the time or the error rate, and the cost per unit, then do the multiplication together: 1,200 invoices a month × 9 minutes = 180 hours a month. When the client gives the numbers, they own the result; a figure you invented will be challenged by the first finance person who sees it. If they do not know a number, agree a range or how to measure it before the next meeting.

Listen for the compelling event: a date or a change that makes acting now necessary (a new ERP, an audit, a merger, a regulation such as mandatory electronic invoicing, a peak season). A real problem without a compelling event often loses to “not now”.
points: Open questions to explore, closed questions to confirm; never leading questions.
SPIN: Situation, Problem, Implication, Need-payoff.
Implication questions connect a problem to money, risk and other people.
Quantify the impact with the client’s own numbers.
Find the compelling event that makes “now” better than “later”.

example.code:
SPIN QUESTIONS, accounts payable automation
Situation   How many supplier invoices do you receive a month?
            Which ERP do you use, and who enters the invoices?
Problem     Where do invoices get stuck today?
            How often does an invoice not match the purchase order?
Implication What happens when an invoice is approved late?
            How does the backlog affect the month-end close?
            Who else feels it: purchasing, suppliers, the CFO?
Need-payoff If invoices were approved within two days, what would
            that free your team to do?
            How would your CFO measure that the problem is solved?

IMPACT, worked with the client
1,200 invoices/month x 9 min = 10,800 min = 180 h/month
example.note: Few situation questions, more implication and need-payoff questions; the numbers come from the client.

lessons.title: Qualification: BANT, MEDDIC and MEDDPICC
text: Qualifying means deciding, with evidence, whether a deal is worth your time and how likely it is to close. BANT, a framework that comes from IBM, checks four things: Budget (is there money, or can it be found?), Authority (who can say yes?), Need (is there a real problem?) and Timeline (when must it be solved?). BANT is quick and suits smaller deals and early SDR qualification; its weakness is that budget is often not set before the business case exists, so treat a “no budget yet” as a question, not a disqualification.

MEDDIC, built for complex enterprise sales, asks for six elements. Metrics: the measurable gain the client expects. Economic buyer: the person who controls the money and can say yes when others say no. Decision criteria: what the options will be judged on. Decision process: the steps, people and dates from now to a decision. Identify pain: the business problem and its cost. Champion: someone inside with power and influence who wants your solution to win and sells it when you are not in the room.

MEDDPICC adds two letters. Paper process: what happens between “yes” and a signed contract (purchasing, legal review, security questionnaire, vendor onboarding, signature levels); it often takes weeks and kills end-of-quarter forecasts. Competition: who else the client is looking at, including the status quo and an in-house build, which are frequent winners.

Use the framework as a checklist of gaps, not a form to fill once. For each letter, write what you know, the evidence and what is missing, then plan how to fill each gap: a question for the next call, a meeting to request, a document to ask for. A deal with an unknown economic buyer and no decision process is not a forecastable deal, whatever the champion says.

Disqualify early and politely when the gaps cannot be filled: no pain worth solving, no access to anyone with authority, or a timing far beyond your horizon. Say it openly (“It sounds like this is not a priority this year; shall we talk again in the spring?”) and set a reminder. Honest qualification makes your pipeline smaller and your forecast right.
points: BANT: Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline; quick, good for early qualification.
MEDDIC: Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion.
MEDDPICC adds Paper process and Competition (status quo and in-house build included).
Track each letter with evidence and a plan to fill the gap.
Disqualify early and politely when the gaps cannot be filled.

example.code:
MEDDPICC - Distributor, AP automation, 36k EUR/year
M  Metrics           Cut approval time from 8 days to 2; recover
                     early-payment discounts           [confirmed]
E  Economic buyer    CFO (signs above 20k)        [not met yet] GAP
D  Decision criteria SAP B1 connector, approval rules, price
                                                      [partly known]
D  Decision process  AP lead -> CFO -> IT check -> purchasing
                                         [dates missing]     GAP
P  Paper process     Security questionnaire + legal review [unknown] GAP
I  Identify pain     Manual keying, late penalties, close on day 8
                                                         [confirmed]
C  Champion          AP lead: wants it, but limited influence  [weak]
C  Competition       Status quo + one local competitor       [known]
Next actions: ask the AP lead to set up 20 min with the CFO;
ask for the security questionnaire now; agree decision dates.
example.note: Each gap has an action; the deal is not forecast as likely until the economic buyer is met.

lessons.title: The buying committee
text: In B2B, several people take part in a purchase, and each looks at it from a different angle. The economic buyer owns the budget and the final yes. Users live with the product every day and care about ease and time saved. IT checks integration, security and data. Purchasing (procurement) compares suppliers and negotiates terms. Legal reviews the contract, liability and data protection (in Europe, the GDPR data processing agreement). Finance checks the business case.

Some people play roles across these titles. The champion has influence and wants you to win; a coach gives you information but may not have power; a blocker prefers the status quo or another supplier. A friendly contact is not automatically a champion: test it by asking them to do something (introduce you to the economic buyer, share the decision process). Someone who will not or cannot is a coach at best.

Map the committee early. For each person, note the role, what they care about, their attitude towards you and how much influence they have, and who you have not met yet. Ask your contact directly: “Apart from you, who will be involved in choosing a solution like this? Who signs? Who could say no?” A short map shows the gaps at a glance, often a missing economic buyer or an IT team nobody has spoken to.

Multi-thread: build contact with several people, not only your main contact. A deal that depends on one person dies when that person is ill, changes job or loses an internal argument. Bring your own people in at the right level: your manager with their manager, your solution engineer with their IT. Always do it with your champion’s agreement, not behind their back.
points: Economic buyer, users, IT, purchasing, legal and finance each judge differently.
Champion = influence + wants you to win; test it with a concrete request.
Map each person: role, priorities, attitude, influence, met or not.
Multi-thread: several contacts, so the deal survives one person leaving.
Go above or around your contact only with their agreement.

example.code:
BUYING COMMITTEE MAP
Name / role        Cares about               Attitude   Influence  Met
CFO (econ. buyer)  Close faster, cash, risk  unknown    high       no
AP lead (champion) Less overtime, no errors  for        medium     yes
AP clerks (users)  Easy screens, no rework   for        low        yes
IT manager         SAP connector, security   neutral    high (veto) no
Purchasing         Price, terms, 3 quotes    neutral    medium     no
Legal              DPA, liability cap        unknown    medium     no

Gaps: CFO and IT not met. Plan: AP lead introduces the CFO this week;
our solution engineer calls the IT manager about the connector.
example.note: The map shows at once who has not been met and where a veto could come from.

lessons.title: The value story and the business case
text: A value story links what the client told you to a measurable result: their situation, the problem, its cost, what changes with your solution and the gain in their own metrics. It is told in their words and numbers, not yours. “You process 1,200 invoices a month by hand, it takes about 180 hours a month and you paid late penalties last quarter; with automated capture and approvals, your team could focus on supplier issues and you close the month earlier.”

Start with the cost of the problem per year. A common formula for time lost is volume × time per unit × loaded cost per hour: 1,200 invoices a month × 12 months × 9 minutes ÷ 60 × 42 € an hour = 90,720 € a year. Add other costs the client confirmed (penalties, lost discounts, errors), but keep each line traceable to a source. A smaller, defensible number beats a large one finance will tear apart.

Then show the return. ROI = (gain − cost) ÷ cost. If the solution saves 90,000 € a year and costs 24,000 € a year plus 6,000 € of setup, year-one ROI = (90,000 − 30,000) ÷ 30,000 = 2, so 200 %. Payback = total cost ÷ monthly gain = 30,000 ÷ 7,500 = 4 months. Many finance teams find payback easier to judge than ROI; give both, and state the assumptions next to the numbers.

Build the business case with your champion and let them present it inside. Count only part of the time saved as a gain when the client will not reduce the team (the time goes to better work, which is real value but not cash), and say so. Conservative assumptions, the client’s own numbers and a clear before / after make the case credible; a spreadsheet full of your guesses makes it a sales document.

In an interview, you may be asked to build a quick business case live. Ask for the volumes and costs, write the formula out loud, round sensibly and finish with the sentence the economic buyer cares about: “For 30,000 € in year one, you recover about 90,000 € of team time and stop paying late penalties; the investment pays back in about four months.”
points: Value story: their situation, problem, cost, change and gain, in their words.
Cost of the problem = volume × time per unit × cost per hour (per year).
ROI = (gain − cost) ÷ cost; payback = cost ÷ monthly gain.
Use the client’s numbers and conservative assumptions, written next to the result.
Let the champion own and present the business case internally.

example.code:
A                              B
1  Item                           Value
2  Invoices per month             1200
3  Minutes per invoice (manual)   9
4  Loaded cost per hour (EUR)     42
5  Cost of the problem per year   =B2*12*B3/60*B4      -> 90,720
6  Annual subscription            24000
7  One-time setup                 6000
8  Year-one cost                  =B6+B7               -> 30,000
9  Year-one ROI                   =(B5-B8)/B8          -> 2.02 (202 %)
10 Payback (months)               =B8/(B5/12)          -> 3.97
example.note: Every number comes from a cell the client can check and change; with the rounded 90,000 € gain, ROI is 200 % and payback 4 months.

lessons.title: Demos that sell
text: A demo is not a product tour. It proves that you can solve the problems found in discovery, so it is built from your notes: the two or three pains that matter most, shown in the order the client cares about. If you have not done discovery, push back politely and ask for twenty minutes of questions first, or open the demo with them. A generic demo to people you know nothing about is the most common way to lose interest in an hour.

Use tell-show-tell for each pain. Tell: remind them of the problem in their words (“You said invoices that don’t match the order wait for days”). Show: the shortest path in the product that solves it, with their kind of data if you can. Tell: confirm the value and check it lands (“So mismatches reach the buyer the same day. How would that change your month-end?”). Then move to the next pain.

Show less. Every extra feature costs attention and can raise new objections or questions from people who were not part of the problem. Leave out what nobody asked about, and keep “one more thing” for a later meeting if it matters. Plan the demo for about half the meeting and keep time for questions and the next step.

Handle questions calmly. Repeat the question to check you understood it, answer briefly, and if you do not know, say so and promise an answer by a date (then keep the promise). When a question is about a feature you do not have, ask why it matters before answering: sometimes it is a must-have, often it is a passing idea. Note who asked what: questions show you the priorities of each person on the buying committee.

Rehearse with a solution engineer if you have one, test the environment and data before the call, and prepare a plan B (screenshots or a recorded flow) for when the live system fails. End the demo the way you end a discovery call: a summary of what they saw against what they needed, and a dated next step.
points: Build the demo from discovery notes, not from the product menu.
Tell-show-tell for each pain: remind, show the shortest path, confirm the value.
Show less: every unasked feature costs attention and invites objections.
Repeat questions, answer briefly, and ask why a missing feature matters.
Rehearse, test, keep a plan B, and end with a dated next step.

example.code:
DEMO PLAN - 45 min, CFO + AP lead + IT manager
0-5    Recap discovery: 3 pains in their words, agree the agenda
5-12   Pain 1 (AP lead): manual keying
       TELL  "Today every invoice is typed by hand, ~9 min each"
       SHOW  upload a PDF invoice -> fields captured -> matched to PO
       TELL  "That's the 180 h/month we discussed. Does it fit?"
12-20  Pain 2 (CFO): approvals take 8 days, late penalties
       SHOW  approval rule by amount, mobile approval, aging dashboard
20-27  Pain 3 (IT): SAP Business One connector and access rights
27-40  Questions (note who asks what)
40-45  Summary against their needs + next step: business case
       review with the CFO on Thu 23 Oct
example.note: Each block maps to one pain and one person; the last five minutes are kept for the next step.

lessons.title: Mutual action plan and next steps
text: A mutual action plan (also called a close plan or success plan) is a shared, dated list of the steps both sides take from today to the start of the project: meetings, demos, security review, business case approval, legal review, signature, kick-off. Each step has an owner on the client side or yours, and a date. You build it with your champion and share it openly; it turns “we’ll get back to you” into a project both sides follow.

Plan backwards from the client’s go-live date, the compelling event. If the new process must work by 1 March and setup takes six weeks, the contract must be signed by mid-January, so the legal review starts early January and the business case goes to the CFO before Christmas. Working backwards shows the client, not you, that the timeline is tight, and it shows you which steps cannot slip.

Deals stall when a step has no owner, no date or no reason. Watch the warning signs: the next step is “send more information”, meetings are moved twice, your champion stops answering, a new person appears late, or purchasing arrives with a request for three quotes you did not know about. React early: go back to the plan with your champion, ask what changed, and if needed ask for a short call with the economic buyer to confirm that the project is still a priority.

When the deal is qualified or signed, hand it over well. An SDR hands a qualified meeting to the account executive with the discovery notes, the people met, the pain in the client’s words and the agreed next step; the client must not have to repeat everything. After signature, the account executive hands the account to customer success or the project team with the business case, the metrics the client expects, the decision makers and any promise made during the sale. A clean handover protects the renewal next year.

Keep the plan, the notes and the next step in the CRM, updated after every meeting. Your manager reads the forecast from it, and the mutual action plan dates are the evidence for the close date you enter.
points: Mutual action plan: shared steps, an owner and a date for each, up to kick-off.
Plan backwards from the client’s go-live date or compelling event.
Stall signs: vague next steps, moved meetings, silent champion, late newcomers.
Handover SDR → AE → customer success with notes, metrics and promises made.
Update the plan in the CRM after every meeting; close dates need evidence.

example.code:
MUTUAL ACTION PLAN - AP automation (go-live 1 March)
Step                               Owner              Date     Status
Demo with CFO, AP lead, IT         Rep + AP lead      14 Oct   done
SAP connector call                 Our SE + IT mgr    21 Oct   done
Business case review               AP lead + CFO      23 Oct   planned
Security questionnaire returned    Our SE             31 Oct   open
Proposal and pricing               Rep                 7 Nov   open
Purchasing review (3 quotes)       Purchasing         21 Nov   open
Legal review: contract + DPA       Their legal + ours  5 Dec   open
Signature                          CFO                15 Dec   open
Kick-off and setup (6 weeks)       Our CS + AP lead    6 Jan   open

HANDOVER NOTE (AE -> customer success)
Goal: approvals in 2 days, close by day 5. Sponsor: CFO.
Promised: SAP B1 connector live by go-live; training for 3 clerks.
example.note: Every step has an owner and a date; the handover repeats the metrics and promises the client will judge you on.

SPIN: collects facts (volumes, tools, team); ask few

SPIN: looks for difficulties and dissatisfaction

pitfalls: Pitching the product in the first minutes instead of asking questions; the client says “send me a deck” and disappears.
Asking a long list of situation questions the website already answers, which tires the client and teaches you nothing new.
Treating a friendly contact as a champion without testing whether they can and will act (meet the economic buyer, share the process).
Building the business case on your own guesses instead of the client’s numbers; finance rejects it at the first question.
Showing every feature in the demo: attention drops and new objections appear from people who had no such problem.
Ending a call without a dated next step, or with “I’ll send you some information”.
Forecasting a deal as likely while the economic buyer, decision process or paper process is still unknown.

exercises.q: Put the steps of a discovery call in order.
steps: Thank them and confirm the time available
Upfront contract: purpose, both agendas and possible outcomes
Questions about their situation and current process
Problems, their impact and who else is affected
Decision process, people involved and timing
Summarize what you heard and let them correct it
Agree a next step with a date and attendees
exercises.answer: Set the frame first (time, upfront contract), then explore from situation to problems and impact, then how they decide. Summarize before asking for the next step, so the next step rests on facts the client confirmed.

exercises.q: Sort these discovery questions into open and closed questions.

groups.name: Open
items: How do supplier invoices reach your team today?
What happens when an invoice does not match the order?
Tell me about your last month-end close.
Why is this a priority now?

groups.name: Closed
items: Do you use SAP Business One?
How many people work in accounts payable?
Is the CFO the one who signs?
Should the project be live before March?

exercises.answer: Open questions make the client explain and reveal what you did not know; closed ones confirm a fact or a number. Discovery leans on open questions and uses closed ones to check details.

exercises.q: Match each MEDDIC letter with its meaning.
pairs: The measurable gain the client expects
The person who controls the budget and gives the final yes
What the options will be judged on
The steps, people and dates up to a decision
The business problem and what it costs
An insider with influence who sells your solution when you are not there
exercises.answer: MEDDPICC adds Paper process (from yes to signature) and Competition (other suppliers, status quo, in-house build).

exercises.q: In SPIN, which of these is an implication question?
options: Do you have problems with invoice approvals?
How does the approval backlog affect your month-end close and your suppliers?
Wouldn’t it be great to approve invoices on your phone?
exercises.answer: An implication question explores the consequences of a problem (on the close, on suppliers, on cost). The first is a situation question, the second a (closed) problem question, and the last a leading question.

exercises.q: In a 30-minute discovery call, you spoke for 18 minutes. What was your talk ratio, in percent?
exercises.answer: 18 ÷ 30 = 0.6, so 60 %. In discovery you spoke more than the client: you were probably pitching. Ask more open questions and let silences last.

exercises.q: MEDDPICC adds two letters to MEDDIC: P for the process from “yes” to signature, and C for the other options the client considers. Complete them.
exercises.snippet:
M E D D P I C C
P = ___ process
C = ___
exercises.answer: P is the Paper process (purchasing, legal, security review, signature levels between “yes” and a signed contract) and the second C is Competition.

exercises.q: Discovery with a mid-sized distributor: your contact is the accounts payable lead, who loves the solution. The CFO signs any purchase above 20,000 €; the deal is 36,000 € a year.

steps.text: Your contact says: “I’ll present it to the CFO myself, no need for you to meet him.” What do you do?

choices.label: Thank them, then ask to prepare it together and join for 20 minutes, to answer the CFO’s questions on cost and risk
choices.feedback: You respect your champion and still reach the economic buyer. A short, prepared meeting with the CFO is the strongest way to protect the deal.

choices.label: Agree and send them the slide deck
choices.feedback: Your contact will present your solution less well than you, and you will not hear the CFO’s objections. Deals often die in meetings the rep did not attend.

choices.label: E-mail the CFO directly without telling your contact
choices.feedback: Going around your champion without their agreement can turn them into a blocker. Multi-thread, but with their consent.

steps.text: The contact agrees. How do you prepare the CFO meeting?

choices.label: Build a one-page business case with the AP lead using their numbers: cost of the problem, cost, ROI, payback
choices.feedback: A CFO judges money and risk. A business case built on the client’s own numbers, and presented with the champion, is credible.

choices.label: Prepare a full product demo of every feature
choices.feedback: The CFO did not ask for a product tour. Show value and risk, and keep the demo to what matters to them.

steps.text: At the end of the meeting, the CFO says: “Interesting, send me a proposal.” What next?

choices.label: Ask what the decision process is from here, who else must approve, and agree dated steps in a mutual action plan
choices.feedback: You turn a vague request into a plan: decision process, paper process and dates. The proposal then lands in a known process.

choices.label: Send the proposal the same evening and wait for an answer
choices.feedback: Without a decision process and dates, the proposal sits in an inbox and the deal stalls.

exercises.answer: A champion is precious but is not the economic buyer. Get access to the decision maker with the champion’s agreement, bring a business case built on their numbers, and leave with a decision process and a mutual action plan, not a vague request.

exercises.q: In B5, the cost of the problem per year: invoices per month × 12 months × minutes per invoice ÷ 60 × cost per hour.
rows: Cost of the problem per year
exercises.hint: Hours per year = invoices × 12 × minutes ÷ 60; then multiply by the cost per hour.
exercises.explain: 1,200 × 12 × 9 ÷ 60 = 2,160 hours a year, × 42 € = 90,720 € a year. Built from the client’s numbers, this is the anchor of the business case.

exercises.q: In B5, the year-one ROI: (annual gain − year-one cost) ÷ year-one cost, where the year-one cost is the subscription plus the setup.
exercises.hint: Year-one cost = B3 + B4. ROI = (gain − cost) / cost.
exercises.explain: Year-one cost = 24,000 + 6,000 = 30,000 €. ROI = (90,000 − 30,000) ÷ 30,000 = 2, so 200 %. Format the cell as a percentage and state the assumptions next to it.

exercises.q: In B5, the payback in months: year-one cost (subscription + setup) ÷ monthly gain.
exercises.explain: 30,000 ÷ (90,000 ÷ 12) = 30,000 ÷ 7,500 = 4 months. Many CFOs find a payback in months easier to judge than an ROI percentage.

exercises.q: In D2, the weighted value of these four opportunities: the sum of each amount × its win probability.
exercises.hint: SUMPRODUCT multiplies the two ranges row by row and adds the results.
exercises.explain: 40,000 × 0.2 + 25,000 × 0.5 + 60,000 × 0.1 + 18,000 × 0.8 = 8,000 + 12,500 + 6,000 + 14,400 = 40,900 €. Weighted value is only as good as the probabilities: tie them to evidence (MEDDPICC gaps filled), not to hope.

exercises.q: In a demo for a CFO, an AP lead and an IT manager, which approach is best?
options: A full tour of the product, menu by menu, so nothing is missed
Tell-show-tell on the three pains found in discovery, then questions and a dated next step
Start with pricing to save everyone’s time
Show the newest features first because they impress most
exercises.answer: Build the demo from discovery: for each pain, remind it in their words, show the shortest path that solves it and confirm the value. Keep time for questions and end with a dated next step.

exercises.q: You sell a meeting-room booking tool (sensors, an app and analytics) to companies with several offices. Write 8 discovery questions you would ask a facilities manager, covering situation, problem, implication, need-payoff and the decision process.
exercises.answer: Situation: 1) How many offices and meeting rooms do you manage, and how are rooms booked today? 2) How many days a week are people on site, on average? Problem: 3) What goes wrong with bookings today (ghost bookings, double bookings, no room when needed)? 4) How do you know how much the rooms are really used? Implication: 5) What does it cost you when rooms are booked but empty, for example office space you rent but do not use, or meetings that start late? 6) How does it affect your decisions on office space, such as a lease renewal or a move? Need-payoff: 7) If you had real usage data per room and per floor, what would you decide differently, and what would that be worth? Decision process: 8) Who else would be involved in choosing a solution like this (IT for the sensors and Wi-Fi, the CFO for the budget, HR), and is there a date, such as a lease renewal, by which you need an answer? Good answers are open, ask about consequences and value, and end with the decision process and a compelling event.

interview.q: How do you run a discovery call?
interview.a: I prepare hypotheses from the website, news, job offers and the person’s profile. I open with an upfront contract: time, purpose, what each side wants and the possible outcomes, including “not a fit”. Then I ask mostly open questions, from their situation to the problems, their impact and who else is affected, and I quantify the impact with their numbers. I ask how they decide and by when. I end with a summary in their words and a next step with a date and attendees, and I log it in the CRM the same day.

interview.q: Explain MEDDIC (or MEDDPICC) and how you use it.
interview.a: Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain and Champion; MEDDPICC adds Paper process and Competition. I use it as a gap list per deal: for each letter, what I know, the evidence and what is missing, with an action to fill each gap. A deal where I have not met the economic buyer or do not know the decision and paper process stays out of my commit forecast.

interview.q: What is the difference between a champion and a friendly contact?
interview.a: A champion has influence, has a personal reason to want the change and acts for you when you are not in the room. A friendly contact may simply enjoy the calls. I test it by asking for something concrete: an introduction to the economic buyer, the decision process, an internal document. If they cannot or will not, they are a coach, and I keep looking for a real champion and multi-thread the account.

interview.q: The prospect says there is no budget. Do you disqualify the deal?
interview.a: Not straight away. Budgets for a new solution often do not exist until the business case does. I check the pain and its cost: if the problem costs them 90,000 € a year and the solution 30,000 €, the question becomes where the money comes from and who can release it, which leads to the economic buyer. If there is no real pain, no authority within reach and no timing, then I disqualify politely and set a reminder.

interview.q: How do you build a business case for a client?
interview.a: With the client and their numbers. I start with the cost of the problem: volume × time × cost per hour, plus confirmed costs such as penalties. I compare it with the full cost (subscription, setup, internal time) and show ROI and payback, for example 200 % ROI and a four-month payback. I keep the assumptions conservative and visible, and I let my champion present it internally so it is their case, not my sales document.

interview.q: How do you prepare a demo?
interview.a: From my discovery notes: the two or three pains that matter and who cares about each. I use tell-show-tell for each pain, show the shortest path, leave out what nobody asked for, and keep half the meeting for questions and the next step. I rehearse with the solution engineer, test the data and keep screenshots as a plan B. I note the questions each person asks, because they show me the buying committee’s priorities.

interview.q: A deal has gone quiet after a good demo. What do you do?
interview.a: I look at what is missing: usually no dated next step, an economic buyer not met or an unknown decision process. I contact my champion with a reason, not “just checking in”: a piece of the business case, a reference customer, or a question about the timeline. I go back to the mutual action plan and ask what changed. If the champion stays silent, I reach another contact I already know in the account, and if the priority has truly gone, I say so and move the deal out of the forecast.

interview.q: How do you hand over a deal to the account executive or customer success?
interview.a: In writing and in a short call: the people met and their roles, the pain in the client’s words, the numbers, the metrics they expect, what was promised and the agreed next step. For a sale that closed, I also share the business case and the decision makers, because customer success will need to prove those metrics before the renewal. The client should never have to repeat their story.
